subtopic: crowds, fairs, and the press of people
sentence: The new year crowd filled the square to its edges and beyond, the whole city pouring in to see the year turn together, and I stood wedged among strangers in the cold, and when the moment came the crowd made one enormous sound, a roar of pure collective gladness, and I made it too. I had no one in that city. For that one shouted minute it did not matter. The crowd had taken me in, as crowds will, and let me belong, briefly, to everyone.

Each night the pilgrim hostel filled with the same weary fellowship, feet bandaged, packs propped, the day's complaints traded like currency, and each morning we scattered along the route at our different paces only to gather again, the same faces, at the next refuge. It was the loosest possible community and one of the truest I have known, bound by nothing but a shared direction and a shared and gradual transformation.

subtopic: crowds, fairs, and the press of people
sentence: The market on its busiest day was almost impassable, a slow hot crush of bodies through the narrow lanes, and you did not so much walk it as get digested by it, and yet the crowd had a courtesy, a give and take, a thousand strangers negotiating the same small space without malice. I let it carry me. It deposited me, eventually, breathless and grinning, out the far end, having shown me, in its press and heat and noise, the city at its most alive.

When the storm closed the pass we sheltered under an overhang of rock, six strangers and a dog, building a fire of whatever the slope offered and feeding it carefully through the worst hours. We did not talk much. The fire was the conversation. By morning the snow had stopped and the world was blinding white and silent, and we put out the fire together, scattering the ash, and went our six ways as if the night had been a thing we had only imagined.

The last bus had gone and the next was at six, so I made a bed of my pack in the corner of the station where the heating pipes ran, and watched the night staff mop the floor in long slow arcs. A man who slept there every night, by the look of his arrangements, nodded to me as one nods to a colleague. I slept in snatches, woke to pigeons and the rattle of the first shutter, and stepped out into a morning that felt earned.

The first walk in a new city is the only one of its kind, the streets all equally unknown, every corner a genuine question, and I gave myself to it that first morning, no map, no aim, just the city teaching me itself one block at a time. I learned the river. I learned the loud street and the quiet one. By dusk the city had become, in my private rough way, mine, and I would never again be able to see it fresh.

I had not meant to spend the night on the beach, but the tide and the dark and a certain pleasant tiredness conspired, and I dug a hollow in the warm sand above the line of weed and lay down in it. The sea kept up its long argument with the shore. A dog appeared from somewhere, considered me, and curled against my back, and we kept each other warm until the fishermen came down at first light to drag their boats to the water.

subtopic: capitals and their grand public spaces
sentence: At night the capital lit its monuments, and the grand square became a stage set, the floodlit columns and domes and the great equestrian statue all glowing against the dark, and the effect was theatrical and beautiful and slightly unreal. The daytime square was a thoroughfare; the night square was a spectacle. I crossed it slowly, the only one not hurrying, taking the free show the city put on for itself every single night, whether anyone watched or not.

I heard the call to prayer five times a day for a month and by the end I no longer heard it as exotic, or as anything but the city's own clock, the sound by which the day was jointed, and on the morning I left, very early, it rose in the dark from a dozen minarets at once, overlapping, and I stood with my bag waiting for the taxi and let the city sing me goodbye in the only voice it had been using all along.

The buried city had been dug from the ash that killed it, and to walk its streets was to walk through an interrupted afternoon, a loaf still in an oven, a dog still at the end of a chain, a graffito still fresh on a wall. The catastrophe had preserved what it destroyed. I stood in a kitchen two thousand years cold and felt, more sharply than in any cemetery, the simple unbearable fact that these had been people, exactly like me, who had not expected the day to end.

subtopic: night arrivals and the dark side of travel
sentence: The train was hours late and put me out in a strange town at midnight, and the romance of travel, which the daytime sustains so easily, drained completely away, and I was just a person far from home, tired, in the dark, in a place that owed me nothing. A taxi driver took pity, or took a fare, and got me to a bed. The town in daylight, the next morning, was charming. The town at midnight had been a different town entirely.

I found my street by the third attempt, having shown the address to three strangers who each pointed with great confidence in three different directions, and the finding of it felt like a small graduation. The room was plain and the window looked at a wall, and yet it was mine, a fixed point at last in the unknown city, and I sat on the bed in the early dark feeling the specific deep relief of having, in a strange place, an address.

subtopic: returning to a place after years
sentence: I had loved the place once and I went back to check whether the love had been the place or the time of life, and the answer, I found, was both, inseparably, and the place without that time of life was just a place, fine, pleasant, but not the place I had carried for years. The magic had not been in the streets. It had been in me, in the particular open hungry self I had been when I first walked them, and that self had not made the return trip.

We ran low on water on the second afternoon and the mood in the vehicle changed without anyone speaking, a tightening, a new attention to the fuel gauge and the sun. The desert does this; it strips travel down to its oldest terms. When we reached the well and it had water, the relief was physical, a loosening of something I had not known was clenched, and we drank and laughed too loudly and were, for an hour, gloriously alive.

The glacier was a frozen river that moved a few inches a year, and walking on it I could hear it, the deep groans and sudden cracks of all that ice in its century-slow descent, and the meltwater ran in blue veins across its surface and vanished, roaring, down shafts to its hidden underside. It was the most alive-seeming dead thing I have stood on. I felt, on the glacier, the planet's geological pulse, slow and vast and entirely uninterested in the brief warm creature it carried.

We took the slow boat because the fast boat is a stupidity, a way of converting a river into a corridor, and the slow boat is a way of letting the river be a river. It stopped where it liked. It drifted. The Mekong went amber in the evenings and the children on the banks were the same children, it seemed, all the way down, and by the end I could not have said where one day's water ended and the next began.

The border town had the particular character of all border towns, a place that faced two ways at once, where two currencies circulated and two languages mixed in the market and the cuisine was a negotiated peace between the kitchens of two countries. People here had relatives on both sides and crossed the line as casually as crossing a street. The town belonged, in the end, not to either nation but to the seam itself, and was the richer and stranger for it.

The last night before flying home I walked the city I was leaving for hours, trying to fix it, to take a final reading, knowing that this was the last time I would see these particular streets as a person who lived in them, however briefly, rather than as a person who had once passed through. The city did not know it was being farewelled. It went about its evening. And I walked it, memorising, the way you memorise a face at a station.

The road was unpaved for two hundred kilometres and the bus took it like a small boat in a swell, and the passengers rode the lurches with the unconscious skill of long practice, swaying as one. Dust came in at every window and settled on everything, on the fruit, on the babies, on me, and by the journey's end we were all the same red colour, a busload of strangers united by the road's indifferent paintwork.

The festival had drumming, and the drumming went on for hours, and it got into the body the way good drumming does, until the crowd was no longer listening to it but moving inside it, a single organism with one enormous pulse. I had not meant to dance and I was dancing. The drums had simply decided. There is a music that bypasses the mind entirely and speaks to something older, and on that hot night, in that crowd, I met it.

He was an old Englishman travelling alone, and he attached himself to our table at dinner with the practised ease of a man who had been doing this for fifty years. He had stories, of course, but the good thing about him was that he also wanted ours, and asked real questions, and remembered the answers. When he left he shook each of our hands and wished us, with great seriousness, good roads, and I have wished it of people ever since.

The lake town had a promenade and the promenade had benches, and the benches were occupied each evening by the same old men in the same order, watching the same water do the same nothing, and finding in it, clearly, an inexhaustible interest. I joined them. The water did nothing. The light changed on it slowly. And I began, by the end of the week, to understand the benches, and the old men, and the particular wealth of having a lake to do nothing in front of.

subtopic: light, dusk, and the changing day
sentence: I watched the mountain change colour through the whole long evening, from grey to gold to a flushed rose to a deep blue and at last to a black silhouette against the stars, and I did almost nothing else for two hours, because the mountain, lit so, was enough, was a whole evening's worth of event. The light did all the work. The mountain merely stood there and let the departing day paint it, one colour after another, for anyone with the patience to watch.

The hostel common room at midnight was a small United Nations: a Korean cook trading recipes with an Italian, a Dutchman mending a Brazilian's rucksack, two Australians arguing happily about a border crossing neither could pronounce. I had come down for water and stayed three hours. There is a particular friendship that forms among people who will never see each other again, frank and fast and weightless, and that room was full of it.

The man who showed me the ruins was not a guide by trade but a farmer whose land they stood on, and his telling of them was therefore not a script but a relationship, a lifetime of living beside the old stones, knowing which ones the sheep sheltered behind and where, as a boy, he had found a coin. The professional guides recite. He remembered. And to be shown a place by someone who simply knows it is the rarest and best of all guiding.

The hill town was a single staircase that branched, and I climbed it by whim, taking the left turn here for no reason and the right there for the look of a cat sunning itself. There is no being lost in such a place, only a slower kind of arriving. I came out on the roof of the town with the valley laid below me and could not have retraced a single step, and would not have wished to.

On the long walk we fell silent, the local man and I, because we had exhausted our tiny shared vocabulary in the first hour, and the silence that followed was not awkward but companionable, two people walking the same road, content to point things out, to share food, to be wordlessly together. I have had emptier conversations in my own language. The walk taught me that company does not, in the end, require talk; it requires only presence, and goodwill, and a shared direction.

subtopic: the food of a place and what it reveals
sentence: The cheese of that valley existed nowhere else, could exist nowhere else, because it was made of that valley's particular grass and that valley's particular weather and that valley's particular slow inherited method, and to eat it was to eat the valley itself, distilled. I bought a wedge from the farm that made it. The cheesemaker did not think of his cheese as remarkable. It was simply the taste of home, and he had given me, in a paper wrapping, a piece of his.

I went into the synagogue, one of the oldest in the country, and the caretaker, an old man with all the time in the world, walked me through its quiet rooms and told me its long story of flourishing and catastrophe and stubborn survival. The light came through high windows onto worn wood. He did not ask my faith and I did not offer it; he was simply glad, I think, to have someone to tell, and I was glad to be told.

I stopped at the café because it had a view and stayed because it had a grandmother, and she fed me beyond all reason and asked, in halting borrowed words, about my journey, and I told her, and she nodded as if my whole route had passed across her terrace before. Perhaps it had. The road went by her door. She had been watching travellers go by it, and feeding the ones who stopped, for the better part of a long life.

subtopic: caravanserai, inns, and lodgings with history
sentence: The guesthouse had been a noble's mansion and then a school and then a barracks and now, faded and gentle, took in travellers, and each of its lives had left a layer: a painted ceiling here, an institutional stair there, a bricked-up door that led nowhere anyone now remembered. My room had been, the owner thought, a library. I slept among the ghosts of its many purposes, and the building seemed glad, at last, to be doing something so simple as sheltering a tired stranger.

The sleeper out of Hanoi rocked us north through a darkness that smelled of coal smoke and wet rice. I lay in the upper berth tracing the rattle of couplings, listening to a woman two compartments down sing softly to a child who would not settle. By the time grey light leaked under the blind, the carriage had filled with the green steam of terraced hills, and the conductor came through with tin cups of tea so strong it tasted of the engine.

I stopped at the café for a reason I have forgotten and remember the café still: the oilcloth on the table, the calendar three years out of date, the radio playing something local and sad, the patient old man who brought my coffee and then sat back down to his own. Nothing happened there. It was simply a half hour, in the middle of a long day, of being still in a small ordinary room in a country not my own, and it was enough, and it was good.

subtopic: the strange and the surreal on the road
sentence: In the middle of the desert, miles from any town, I came upon a single telephone box, painted red, perfectly maintained, standing alone in all that sand with its door slightly ajar, and there was no explanation, and no one to ask, and I have never found one. The road delivers these things. The strange does not announce itself; it simply stands there, in the sand, beside the highway, declining utterly to make sense.

The monastery clung to a crag above the valley and the monks had lived their slow life there for a thousand years, and a guest could stay if a guest kept the silence. I stayed two nights. The bells divided the dark into offices. The food was plain and the cell was bare, and in the great hush between the prayers I found a quality of rest I had not known I was starving for, and left reluctantly, and changed.

subtopic: roads, paths, and the act of moving itself
sentence: The country road did not hurry and would not let you hurry, and so it taught a pace, the pace of looking, of noticing the hedge and the gate and the cloud, and I gave myself to that pace and the day grew longer and richer for it. We have built fast roads to defeat distance, and they do, but they defeat the country too, blur it, cancel it. The slow road keeps the country. The slow road, in fact, is the country, unrolling at the speed a person can actually receive it.

subtopic: the smell and texture of place
sentence: Every city announces itself first to the nose, and this one was woodsmoke and frying garlic and the green river smell of a canal, all braided together and unmistakable. I could have found my way back to my room by scent alone, turning at the bakery, again at the tannery I learned to breathe shallowly past, and into the lane where a jasmine had been allowed to overrun a wall and forgave the street everything.

The first night in a new city I always sleep badly, the unfamiliar sounds keeping a part of me on watch, the trams and the strange birds and the particular rhythm of a foreign traffic, and I lay awake learning the city by ear. By the third night the sounds had become a lullaby, the city's voice no longer alien, and I understood that I had crossed, in those three nights, the small invisible border between visiting a place and beginning, however briefly, to live in it.

There was a Japanese man cycling the length of the continent, and we crossed paths three times in three countries, purely by chance, the way ships are said to. The first time we were strangers, the second acquaintances, the third old friends, the gaps between filled in by the simple fact of the road carrying us both the same way. The fourth crossing never came. I still scan the cyclists on every long road, half-hoping.

The small town had one of everything, one church, one school, one bar, one shop, one bus a day, and the economy of it, the lack of all surplus and choice, was itself a kind of clarity. Life here was not a menu. It was a given. I walked the single main street in twenty minutes and then walked it again, slower, and the town, which the guidebook had not mentioned, taught me more about the region than the region's celebrated capital had managed in three days.

subtopic: roads, paths, and the act of moving itself
sentence: At the end of the long day's road there is a tiredness that is also a kind of fullness, the body spent and the mind quiet and the country, all of it, the whole day's worth, settled somewhere inside, and I have lain down at the end of such days in rough beds in strange towns and felt richer than money has ever made me. The road takes the day and gives it back transformed, as distance, as memory, as the particular deep rest that only honest motion earns.

The old farmer wanted, very much, to tell me something, and lacking any shared word he took me by the arm and walked me to it, to a view, to a tree, to a particular spot, and showed me with his whole body what his mouth could not say, and I understood: this was his place, and he loved it, and he wanted, before I left, for me to know that. I knew it. Some things are better said by being walked to than by being spoken.

subtopic: night arrivals and the dark side of travel
sentence: The night ferry docked at four in the morning and decanted us, the foot passengers, onto a black quay in a country we did not know, and we stood there in a confused tired cluster, no buses, no taxis, no plan, the romance of the sea crossing entirely behind us. Travel has these hours. They are not in the photographs. We waited for the dawn together, strangers, cold, and the dawn, when it came, returned us to being travellers rather than merely the stranded.

subtopic: hot springs, baths, and bathing culture
sentence: The onsen sat in a gorge where the river steamed, and the bathing was outdoors, in stone pools at the snow's edge, the contrast of the scalding water and the freezing air a kind of exquisite shock. I soaked in silence, the etiquette here being one of quiet, and watched the steam rise and the snow fall into it and vanish, and felt the long road's tensions dissolve out of my shoulders into the volcanic, ancient warmth.

The frontier between the two countries was a striped pole, a tin shed, and a soldier so young he was still growing into his uniform. I handed over my passport and watched him work through it page by page, sounding out the stamps like a boy reading aloud. Behind him the same hills rolled on, indifferent to the line we had all agreed to draw across them, and a goat wandered through no-man's-land cropping the grass of two nations at once.

subtopic: roads, paths, and the act of moving itself
sentence: The track petered out into open hillside and I kept going anyway, off the path now, making my own way, and there was a particular thrill in that, in the moment a route runs out and the country itself becomes the route, and you navigate by slope and instinct and the look of the land. The path had been a kind of permission. Beyond its end I needed none. I walked the trackless hill in the wind, free of the road, which is its own and rarer pleasure.

subtopic: the strange and the surreal on the road
sentence: The village clock struck thirteen, distinctly, and no one in the square so much as looked up, and when I mentioned it the café owner said yes, it had always done that, the thirteenth strike, and that was simply the clock, and the village had long ago stopped finding it remarkable. I found it remarkable for both of us. The road shows you a place's strangeness fresh, the strangeness its own inhabitants have worn smooth with familiarity and ceased to see.

subtopic: why we go, and the question of travel itself
sentence: I travel, I have decided, because it is the closest thing I have found to a cure for the great human disease of taking the world for granted, and the road, the genuine unfamiliar road, performs that cure reliably: it makes everything strange again, and strangeness is only another word for being properly, fully awake to a thing. I go to be woken. I come home awake. And then, slowly, home puts me back to sleep, and I have to go again.

The aurora came out while we waited for it in the cold, a curtain of green light that rippled and reached and folded across the whole northern sky, silent, slow, indifferent, and the small group of us stood with our heads back making the involuntary sounds people make. I had crossed half the world to see it and it owed me nothing and it gave me everything, and then, after an hour, it faded, and we went in, changed, to the stove and the dark.

The reef under the snorkel mask was a city in full riot, fish in colours that seemed a kind of shouting, a turtle ploughing past with ancient patience, the coral itself alive and reaching. I floated above it for an hour, weightless, breathing through a tube, an awkward visitor to a world that managed its dazzling business with no reference to me whatsoever, and surfaced reluctant, blinking, returned to the dull dry country of air.

subtopic: light, dusk, and the changing day
sentence: There is a particular light, ten minutes long, that comes just after sunset in clear weather, when the whole sky glows and the land below it is lit by no direct source but by the glowing sky itself, shadowless, even, gentle, and it is my favourite light in the world. I have stood still for it in many countries. It asks nothing and gives everything, this brief afterglow, this last soft exhalation of the day, and then it fades, and the stars come, and the travelling evening properly begins.

subtopic: returning to a place after years
sentence: Going back, I found the people had aged exactly as much as I had, which I had somehow not expected, the boy now a man with children, the woman now grey, the old man now gone, and the reunion was warm and strange and shadowed by the arithmetic. We had all kept moving, in our separate places, and now here we were, comparing the distances, and the place that had once held us all young held us now, kindly, in our middle age.

The penguins came ashore in the evening in a small determined crowd, having spent the day at sea, and they walked up the beach past our quiet group with the busy self-importance of commuters, ignoring us utterly. To watch a wild animal go about its ordinary business, unbothered by your existence, is a rarer gift than to watch it perform; the penguins were not a spectacle, they were simply, gloriously, going home.

subtopic: hot springs, baths, and bathing culture
sentence: The bathhouse was a tall echoing room of tile and steam, and the ritual was strict and silent: rinse, soak, rinse again, the body slowly opened and emptied by the heat. Old men sat submerged to the chin with their eyes closed, in a meditation that needed no name. I joined them, found the silence was not awkward but companionable, and left an hour later feeling I had attended a service in a religion that asked nothing but cleanliness.

subtopic: why we go, and the question of travel itself
sentence: Travel does not make you wise, despite what is claimed for it; I have met fools who had been everywhere and sages who had been nowhere. But it does, if you let it, make you humble, by showing you, again and again, how many ways there are to live, to eat, to pray, to be happy, none of them yours, all of them sufficient. That is what I go for, in the end: not wisdom, but the humbling, which is rarer, and harder, and worth the fare.

I liked the border town for the same reason I liked all border towns: it was a place with no fixed identity, and so it had been forced to become interesting, to make a culture out of mixture, a cuisine out of compromise, a daily life out of the constant low friction of the line. The capital cities of both countries were sure of themselves and therefore dull. The frontier town was sure of nothing, and therefore alive.

The grandmother at the corner stall had a face like a walnut and hands that never stopped, and she fed half the neighbourhood from a single charcoal grill, knowing every regular's order without asking. I became, over a week, a minor regular myself, and on the last day she added something extra to my plate, a small wordless gift, and would not say what it was, and it was delicious, and I have wondered ever since.

Dawn at the floating market is a slow collision of boats, each piled with pomelos or chillies or coconuts, the women paddling them standing up with a single oar. Trade happens hull to hull, money and fruit passed across the gap. I drank a coffee handed up from a boat with a charcoal stove in it, sweetened thick with condensed milk, and watched the canal fill with colour as the light came on like something switched.

subtopic: hot springs, baths, and bathing culture
sentence: In that country the evening bath was a non-negotiable institution, and the small inn heated its tub at dusk, and the act of soaking before dinner was as fixed as dinner itself. I came to look forward to it the way one looks forward to sleep, the hot water dissolving the day's walking, and to understand that a culture which builds such a pause into every single day knows something about being alive that my own hurried country has forgotten.

Breakfast in that city was a thing you ate walking, bought from a window, a hot parcel of dough and egg pressed into your hand by someone who had been awake since four, and the whole working population moved through the dawn streets eating it, a city feeding itself on the move. I joined the flow, parcel in hand, and felt, for the length of that breakfast, entirely and happily a local.

The migration crossed the river while we watched, ten thousand wildebeest pouring down the bank and into the current in a churning desperate flood, the crocodiles waiting, the dust and the noise and the sheer animal urgency of it almost too much to take in. It was not beautiful. It was something older and harder than beautiful. It was the planet doing what it has always done, indifferent and immense, and we were lucky beyond words to see it.

We left before dawn to beat the heat, and the desert at that hour was a country of long blue shadows that shortened as we drove until, by ten, there were no shadows at all and the dunes burned white. The driver navigated by landmarks I could not see and rhythms I could not feel. At the well at noon we found three other vehicles and an unspoken brotherhood of people who understood that out here you stop, you share water, you ask after the road ahead.

From the top of the pass I could see the road I had spent all morning climbing, looped below me like a dropped ribbon, and the road I had still to descend, looped the same way into the next valley, and between them, where I stood, the high cold hinge of the whole journey. A condor turned overhead, level with me, unbothered. I drank from my bottle and felt, briefly and intensely, the achievement of altitude.

For three days the town belonged to the festival, and the festival belonged to no one in particular, which is what made it a festival. Strangers pressed sweets on me. A man I had never met taught me the steps of a dance everyone but me already knew. At night the square filled with lanterns and the band played until the players themselves were swaying, and I went to bed each dawn having understood nothing and enjoyed everything.

When the storm cut the island off for three days, the islanders showed no concern at all, because being cut off was simply a thing islands did, a few times a year, and the island held everything it needed to wait one out. I waited it out with them. The shop's shelves thinned. The talk in the pub turned to other storms. And the island, sealed by the sea, became briefly the entire and self-sufficient world, which it had perhaps always secretly been.

The villages along the pilgrim route had been receiving walkers for centuries and had a practised, weathered kindness about it, a fountain placed just where the thirst would peak, a bench in just the right shade. The locals waved without stopping their work. We were not events to them; we were weather, a seasonal flow of footsore strangers, and there was a comfort in being so gently and so thoroughly expected.

The pilgrims came in all conditions, the devout and the broken and the merely curious, and the path made no distinction, asking the same blisters of everyone. I had set out for no clear reason and found, somewhere around the third hundred kilometres, that the reason was the walking itself, the meditative monotony of it, the way it emptied the mind of everything but the next ridge and the next village and the slow accumulation of distance into meaning.

A small girl sold me a single flower in the market with such gravity and such a good business sense that I bought three, and she counted my coins twice, and gave me a smile at the end of the transaction that was worth more than all the flowers. I carried them for the rest of the day, wilting, absurd, and could not bring myself to put them down, because they were the receipt of a meeting I did not want to be over.

subtopic: roads, paths, and the act of moving itself
sentence: I have a weakness for the road that goes nowhere in particular, the minor road, the road the maps draw thin, because the major roads go to the major places and the minor roads go to the country itself, to the farm, the hamlet, the river, the long view, the actual texture of a land. I take the thin road whenever I can. It is slower and it is better, and it has shown me, over the years, a hundred places that had no name and needed none, and were enough.

subtopic: returning to a place after years
sentence: I returned to the city expecting to feel at home and felt instead like a tourist with unusually good directions, knowing the streets but no longer known by them, and the loneliness of that was specific and unforeseen. You cannot return to a place you have left; you can only visit the place that has replaced it. The city was glad enough to have me. But it had filled the space I once occupied, as a sea fills a footprint, and there was no longer a shape there that was mine.

I reached the ruined city in the early light before the buses, and for an hour it was mine, the toppled columns and the grass-grown amphitheatre and the temple still somehow standing, all of it silent except for birds. To be alone in such a place is to feel time as a physical pressure. I sat in the empty theatre where ten thousand had once sat, and the silence where their voices had been was the loudest thing I have heard.

There is a particular tiredness at the end of a long walking day that is not like any other tiredness, a clean depletion, a body that has been honestly used, and the meal that follows it tastes the way no other meal tastes. I learned to walk for that tiredness and that meal, and for the sleep after, dreamless and total, and for the morning when the body, against all reason, was somehow ready to do it all again.

The islanders spoke a dialect the mainland found quaint and they found simply their language, and they kept festivals the mainland had forgotten, and they were proud and wary and kind in the particular layered way of people who have been, for centuries, slightly apart. The sea had preserved them, the way amber preserves things. I was a visitor to a place the modern world had reached late and lightly, and I trod carefully, and was grateful.

The houses of the old quarter leaned toward each other across the lanes until their upper floors nearly touched, and the sky was reduced to a bright crooked ribbon overhead, and the light came down filtered, golden, the way light comes into a forest. The quarter had grown like a forest too, slowly, organically, each house finding its space among the others. I walked its dim warm canyons and felt the city's great age settle around me like a coat.

The lighthouse keeper's cottage was the last building on the island, and beyond it only rock and the long fall of the sea, and I walked out to it in the wind feeling I had reached an edge, a genuine end of things. The keeper was automated away years ago. The cottage stood empty, facing the weather. I sat in its lee and looked at the horizon, at all that water, and understood the island, finally, as a held breath between immensities.

I found the stall by the queue, which is always the right way to find a stall, and joined the locals waiting for a woman who had been making one dish, only one, at that corner for thirty years. She did not look up. The dish, when it came, was a paper bowl of something fried and herbed and impossibly good, eaten standing on the pavement, and I understood that I had just had the best meal of the trip and it had cost me less than a coffee.

subtopic: the food of a place and what it reveals
sentence: The festival food was different from the everyday food, richer, rarer, the dishes that the year had been saving up for, and to be in the town on the feast day was to taste what the place considered a treat, a celebration, a splurge, and that told me something tender about it, about its idea of joy. The everyday food shows you a place's character. The festival food shows you its dreams, and I ate the town's dreams, that day, and they were sweet, and fried, and shared.

subtopic: the smell and texture of place
sentence: Rain in that country was not an event but a climate, a constant soft conversation between sky and ground, and within a day I had stopped noticing it and within two I had started to love it. It greened everything, dripped from every eave, beaded on the wool of every sheep, and made the indoors, when you reached it, a small triumph of orange light and steam and the smell of wet dog and woodsmoke.

The flood had come, as it came every year, and the river had spread itself across the whole delta, and the villages stood up out of the brown water on their stilts and their raised mounds, islanded, connected now only by boat, and the people went about their flooded lives with the calm of long practice. I travelled among them by boat and saw that the flood was not a disaster here but a season, expected, even needed, the river simply doing the thing the delta had been shaped by it to do.

The bus was meant for thirty and carried sixty, plus crates of fruit, two goats, and a wedding's worth of folded chairs lashed to the roof, and it ground up the mountain road in second gear with a patience I came to find moving. Every passenger knew every other. The driver stopped for anyone who flagged him, and for lunch, and once simply to admire a view, and the journey took all day, and was, in the end, the destination.

subtopic: photographing and trying to capture a place
sentence: I have a photograph of the village and it tells almost none of the truth: not the woodsmoke, not the cold, not the way the old woman pressed bread on me, not the dog, not the silence after the bus had gone. The photograph shows roofs. The village was everything that happened between the roofs, and no camera has ever been built that can be pointed at that, and so I keep the photograph and distrust it, and keep the rest in my head.

subtopic: capitals and their grand public spaces
sentence: The capital's central park was the lung the dense city breathed through, and on a warm afternoon the whole population seemed to be in it, lying on the grass, rowing the lake, walking the long designed avenues of trees, and the park, which an old regime had built as a pleasure ground for the few, now belonged, unanswerably, to everyone. I lay on the democratic grass among them and felt the city, in the park, at its happiest and most itself.

The pass had been the only way through the range for as long as there had been people on either side of it, and the path that crossed it was worn into the rock by all the millennia of feet and hooves that had braved it. I walked up it slowly, breathing hard, and at the top found a small shrine, a place to give thanks, and understood why: to cross such a place was, in any century, an achievement, and the gratitude of the survivors had pooled here, on the cold summit, for a thousand years.

In the mountain village the men sang after dinner, unaccompanied, a harmony so practised it sounded like one large voice, and the song was clearly old and clearly sad and clearly theirs, and I sat in the corner of the room not understanding a word and understanding everything. Music is the one language the traveller never needs translated. The song told me the village's whole history of hard winters and lost sons, and I have it still.

subtopic: crowds, fairs, and the press of people
sentence: The village fair was small, the whole crowd a few hundred people who all knew each other, and I, the one stranger, was conspicuous and, after the first hour, included, drawn into the games and the eating and the dancing by a community that had decided, collectively and without discussion, to absorb me. A small crowd cannot stay anonymous. It noticed me, considered me, and took me in, and I danced badly in a field with a village that, for one evening, lent me its belonging.

At this height the weather was a personality, mercurial and immediate: sun, then a swift grey ambush of cloud, then snow in July, then sun again, all within an hour. The town had learned to take it without comment. Doors stood ready to be shut. Washing was an act of optimism. I came to admire the equanimity of a people who lived so close to the sky that the sky was practically a neighbour, and a moody one.

The storm came up the valley toward me with a visible front, a wall of grey dragging its rain like a curtain, and I watched it come from the dry side of the line and then it crossed the line and I was in it, drenched in seconds, laughing, because there is a particular exhilaration in being caught honestly out in weather, in having the sky simply happen to you with no roof in the argument.

subtopic: caravanserai, inns, and lodgings with history
sentence: The pilgrim hospice had been giving beds to walkers for eight hundred years, and the practice had worn the place into a particular shape, a courtesy worn smooth as the stone steps. A volunteer washed my feet, an old custom he performed without ceremony or comment, and gave me bread and a bunk in a long room of bunks. I lay there among strangers in the dark, one more pilgrim in an unbroken chain of them, and felt held by the sheer weight of the precedent.

The best afternoons are the ones with no destination, when you put the map away and walk on the principle that any direction is the right one because all of them are unknown. I did this in a city whose name I will keep, and was rewarded with a courtyard of cats, a man repairing accordions, a view I could never find again, and the particular lightness that comes of being, for a few hours, genuinely and happily without a plan.

The temple had been swallowed by the forest and then, painstakingly, recovered from it, and the great roots still gripped the stones like the forest's reluctant signature on the lease. I walked the long causeway in the heat with the carvings unrolling beside me, kings and gods and battles, a whole civilisation's idea of itself in stone, and felt the particular vertigo of standing in the achievement of a people entirely gone.

The two of us communicated entirely through a third language, neither of ours, a few hundred words of trade-route English that we both held imperfectly, and there was something fitting in that, two strangers meeting on the neutral ground of a borrowed tongue. We discussed prices, then politics, then, haltingly, our lives. The borrowed language was just enough. It is astonishing, I have found, how little language two willing people actually need.

I had been gone long enough that home, when I reached it, had the faint strangeness of a place remembered rather than known, the rooms a little smaller, the light a little different, my own street briefly the street of a stranger. It passed within a day. Home reabsorbed me. But for that one day I saw my own life from the outside, with a traveller's eye, and what I saw was that it was, after all, and despite everything, a good place to have come back to.

The hut on the ridge was first-come and already full, so I unrolled my mat on the porch with two other latecomers, and we lay in a row under the eaves like coins in a slot. The cold came up through the boards. Above us the sky was an outrageous spill of stars, and one of the strangers, a Czech woman, named the constellations softly in her own language until the third of us was asleep, and then, I think, until I was too.

subtopic: the smell and texture of place
sentence: The market quarter was a single overwhelming texture, a press of cloth and copper and skin, of hands on your sleeve and voices in your ear and the slick of fish water underfoot. There was no still point in it and no silence. I learned to read it the way you learn to read surf, to find the rhythm and ride it, and after an hour of resistance and an hour of surrender I came out the far side exhilarated and somehow rinsed.

At night the desert gave back the day's heat slowly through the sand, and I lay on it as on a cooling stove, watching satellites cross a sky so crowded with stars it had texture, like sand itself. A jackal called once, far off. The driver slept the instant sleep of a man who trusted the place. I lay awake a long while, not from fear but from a kind of greed, not wanting to miss any of it.

The minibus filled and then, against all apparent physics, kept filling, until I had a stranger's child asleep on my shoulder and a stranger's chicken regarding me from a basket at my feet, and we were all of us packed into a single shared and jolting fate. There is an intimacy forced on you by such travel that the comfortable traveller never knows, and by the journey's end the strangers were no longer quite strangers.

Storm-bound, the ferry sat in harbour for two days, and the island it served and the mainland it left both simply waited, joined and separated by the same weather. I walked the harbour wall in the wind, watching the swell explode white against the light, and felt the particular peace of having my plans cancelled by something so much larger than my plans. When the boat finally sailed the sea was glassy, apologetic, and unbelievably calm.

We sailed into the fjord and the cliffs closed around the ship until the sky was a blue ribbon directly overhead, and waterfalls came down the rock walls in white threads from snowfields we could not see. The water was black and so still it doubled everything. No one on deck spoke above a murmur. The scale of it made conversation feel like litter, and so we all just stood and looked, which was the only sensible response.

The mosque's courtyard was vast and cool and floored with stone worn smooth, and the faithful came and went in the soft rhythm of the prayer hours, and between those hours the great space held a silence so deep it felt like a presence. I sat against a pillar in the shade, removed my shoes as the custom asked, and let the calm of the place, which asked nothing of my own beliefs, simply be offered and simply accepted.

The inland sea was so vast it had its own horizon and its own moods, and the lakeside towns called it the sea and meant it, and treated it with the wariness coastal people give the ocean. I walked its shore for a day and the far side never came into view. Gulls worked the shallows. It smelled, faintly and impossibly, of salt, and I understood that a body of water large enough simply becomes a sea, by acclamation, regardless of the maps.

subtopic: crowds, fairs, and the press of people
sentence: The pilgrimage crowd was the largest gathering I have ever stood in, a human mass that stretched beyond seeing in every direction, and instead of the panic I expected there came a strange peace, a sense of the individual self briefly dissolving into something vast and shared. The crowd had one purpose and I, for that day, borrowed it. We moved together, breathed together, an ocean of strangers made briefly one by a shared direction, and it was, unexpectedly, beautiful.

The petrol station on the desert road had a café attached, and the café had a cat and a card game and a kettle always on, and it was, for the drivers who crossed that emptiness, less a business than an oasis, a fixed warm point in all the blank. We stopped, and were absorbed into the card game, and left an hour later than we meant, and richer for it, the way an unplanned hour always leaves you richer.

The river was the border and the ferry was a man with a pole, and he took me across at the price of a conversation about the rains. On the far bank the customs house had no glass in its windows and a typewriter on the desk, and the officer carbon-copied my details into a ledger that went back, by the look of it, decades. I thought of all the names in that book, everyone who had ever stood where I stood, wanting only to be on the other side.

The sun did not set, and so the days lost their joints, and I found myself walking at what should have been midnight in a light like late afternoon, the whole north awake around me, birds singing, the land glowing. The body rebelled at first and then surrendered. Time, up here in the summer, was a suggestion. I slept when tired, walked when not, and lived for a while in a single enormous day that the calendar insisted, against all evidence, was several.

On the Caledonian sleeper the steward had warned me the dawn would be worth waking for, and it was. Rannoch Moor unrolled outside the window in a sheet of bog cotton and standing water, the sky the colour of a pewter spoon. I drank my coffee standing in the corridor, the carriage swaying like a slow boat, and thought how rare it is now to arrive somewhere having watched the whole country slide beneath you.

I hired a boy to guide me through the medina and got, for the small fee, not just directions but a whole apprenticeship in the place: which tea was good, which shop honest, which lane led where, the medina's working knowledge that no map carries. He delivered me, at the end, to my door, and to a far better understanding of the city, and I have thought since that I should have paid him a great deal more, for he had taught, not merely led.

subtopic: light, dusk, and the changing day
sentence: The northern summer light did not properly end, and so the dusk went on for hours, a long luminous lingering, the sky a slow gradient that never quite resolved into night, and I found I could not go to bed, could not bear to, with the country still so softly, endlessly lit. I walked instead, for hours, through the long pale evening that would not become night, and felt the strange gift of a place where the day, generously, simply refused to be over.

I took the boat to the small island simply because it was there, a low green shape on the horizon that the larger island ignored, and found on it forty people, a chapel, a beach of white sand, and a silence so complete I could hear my own blood. The boatman would come back for me at five. Between the leaving and the coming I had the island almost to myself, and I have rarely felt so far from everything, or so glad of it.

Nothing remained of the town but its outline in the turf, the streets visible as shallow channels, the houses as faint rectangular ghosts, and a single standing arch the centuries had not quite managed to bring down. I walked what had been the main street with the sheep that grazed it now, and tried to people it, to hear the market, and could not, and the failure was itself a kind of knowledge.

The dormitory had eight beds and eight nationalities, and the unspoken treaty among us governed the light, the snoring, the small hours' return of the late. We were not friends and did not pretend to be, but there was a courtesy in that room, a recognition that we were all far from home and all, therefore, owed something. In the morning we nodded and scattered, and the treaty dissolved, having served.

I waited for the ferry in a café where the tide was the only clock anyone consulted, and the woman behind the counter could tell from the colour of the water how rough the crossing would be. Rough, she said, and was right. The boat bucked the channel for forty minutes while a small dog skidded the length of the deck and a child laughed at every lurch, and I held the rail and grinned and was, briefly, ten years old.

The temple complex unfolded courtyard within courtyard, each one quieter than the last, the noise of the city filtering down to nothing, until in the innermost garden there was only the sound of a single bamboo pipe tapping water into a stone basin. I sat on the worn wooden veranda where pilgrims had sat for centuries and did nothing at all, and the doing of nothing, in that place, felt like the most purposeful thing I had done in months.

The woman spoke not a word I knew and yet over the meal she made it entirely clear that I was too thin, that I should eat more, that my journey was foolish and my mother must worry, and all of this came across with perfect clarity through tone and gesture and the universal grammar of a concerned older woman. Language, I have learned, is only the top layer of communication. Beneath it people are remarkably, reliably, legible.

The wheat was ready and the whole plateau was the colour of a lion, and the wind came across it in long visible waves, the field bending and rising like a single golden animal breathing. There was nothing else, no tree, no house, only the wheat and the wind and the enormous sky, and the road I was on ran through the middle of it dead straight to a horizon that the heat made tremble. I have seen mountains that moved me less.

subtopic: capitals and their grand public spaces
sentence: The grand boulevard had been laid out by an emperor who wanted his capital to rival the great cities of the world, and it did, and the trees were enormous and the buildings were palaces and the whole long perspective was a triumph of will and money and a certain ruthless vision. I admired it. I also thought of the old crowded quarter the boulevard had been cut through to make, the lanes and the lives erased to clear this magnificent line, and the admiration cooled, a little, as it should.

subtopic: crowds, fairs, and the press of people
sentence: The harvest fair gathered the scattered farms of the whole high valley into one field, once a year, and the crowd was therefore a kind of reunion, neighbours who lived miles apart and saw each other rarely all crowding in at once, and the noise of it was the noise of a community briefly, gladly, assembled. I stood at the edge of all that gathering and felt the particular tender thing it was: a place too sparse to crowd, crowding, for one day, on purpose, for the joy of it.

subtopic: the strange and the surreal on the road
sentence: At the crossroads in the middle of the plain there was a hotel, a large grand hotel, with a doorman and lit windows and the sound of a piano, and no town for fifty miles in any direction, and no road but the one I was on, and I did not stop, and I have wondered ever since whether I should have. The road offers these doors. It sets them in the emptiness and lights them and leaves it entirely to you whether to find out what is inside.

The town sat at four thousand metres and I arrived breathless, every staircase a negotiation, the thin air a constant quiet reminder of where I had come to. The light up here was merciless and pure, and the colours under it seemed to vibrate. People moved slowly, and I learned to move slowly with them, and found that the altitude, which punished the body, somehow rewarded the eye, sharpening everything it took away the breath to look at.

I came home and for weeks the journey kept surfacing, a smell would do it, a slant of light, a word, and I would be back, briefly, completely, on some road, in some room, and then home would reassert itself. The trip did not end at the door. It went on ending for months, releasing itself slowly, and I let it, because the slow ending was, in its way, a continuation, the journey insisting on being remembered before it would consent to be over.

The two halves of the divided town had once been one town, and you could still see it, the same architecture on both sides of the river that was now a border, the same family names, the same church spires built by the same vanished bishopric. History had cut the town in two with a line, and the line had hardened, and now each half was a foreign country to the other, close enough to wave across, and waving was, mostly, all that was allowed.

We crossed the frozen river on a road that was simply the ice itself, marked with poles, and the strangeness of driving on water, of the river beneath us holding the weight of the truck in its winter discipline, never quite stopped feeling like a transgression. The ice creaked and boomed, settling, doing whatever ice does. The driver was unconcerned. The river would be a road until spring, and then, with no fuss, it would be a river again.

subtopic: hot springs, baths, and bathing culture
sentence: The bath was wood and the water was hot beyond comfort and then, suddenly, exactly right, and through the small window I could see snow on the cedars and a single lantern swinging. The innkeeper had heated it for me alone. To be given a private hour in such water, after weeks on hard roads, was a kindness so complete that I lay there near tears, undone by warmth, by quiet, by the simple fact of being looked after.

We pulled over at a café that was really someone's front garden, tables set out among the chickens, and the family that lived there simply expanded, when travellers stopped, into hosts. The food came from the garden it was served in. A child practised English on me with shy persistence. We had meant to stop for ten minutes and stayed an hour, and drove on full and slightly dazed by the abundance of an entirely unplanned welcome.

subtopic: why we go, and the question of travel itself
sentence: People ask me why I go, and I have never had a single answer, only a handful of partial ones: to see, to be changed, to feel the world's largeness, to escape my own small life and return to it altered. The truest answer is probably the simplest and the least respectable: that I am happy on the road in a way I have never managed to be anywhere else, and that this happiness, unaccountable and reliable, is reason enough, and has had to be.

I met him in the queue for the only working ATM in town, a Argentine who had been on the road for two years and spoke of it without a trace of boastfulness, as a man might speak of a job he happened to have. We ate together that night, and again the next, and then his bus came and mine did not, and that was that. I never learned his surname. I think of him more often than I think of people I have known for decades.

subtopic: the food of a place and what it reveals
sentence: The first meal in a new country is a kind of greeting, and I take it seriously, choosing not the safe thing but the local thing, the dish the place is known by, and eating it carefully, attentively, as one might listen to a first sentence. This country's first sentence to me was a bowl of soup, sour and hot and complicated, and it told me at once that this would be a place of strong opinions and long traditions, and the rest of the trip, in flavour after flavour, bore the soup out.

subtopic: photographing and trying to capture a place
sentence: The most beautiful thing I saw on the whole journey I did not photograph, because it lasted four seconds: a flock of birds turning all at once over a flooded field at dusk, the light catching their undersides, the whole flock flashing silver and then gone. There was no time for the camera and I am glad. The moment is mine, uncropped, unshareable, slightly fading, and entirely, perfectly, mine.

The northern light in winter was a long blue twilight that served as both dawn and dusk, the sun never quite arriving, the day a single extended hesitation between dark and dark, and it should have been depressing and was instead, somehow, beautiful, a country lit like the inside of a sapphire. The villagers had made their peace with it. They lit their windows gold against the blue, and the gold and the blue together, seen from the cold road, were the colours of a kind of stubborn human hope.

The delta was a country still being made, the river dropping its load of mountains here at the sea's edge, building new land, drowning old, and the people who lived on it had learned to live with that uncertainty, to build light, to move, to treat the ground itself as a kind of slow tide. I travelled it by boat, because there was no other honest way, and the delta unrolled, half land and half water and entirely alive, and refused, gloriously, to hold still.

subtopic: light, dusk, and the changing day
sentence: The blue hour, the brief deep dusk after the sun is gone and before the dark is complete, was the loveliest time in the city, the buildings still visible but the lights now on, the sky a colour with no good name, and I learned to be out in it, walking, every evening, for those twenty minutes. The day-city and the night-city are two cities. The blue hour is the bridge between them, and to walk it is to be, for a little while, in both at once.

I spent two days in the frontier town waiting for a permit, and grew fond of its in-between quality, its shops full of the goods of both countries, its café where the talk slid between languages mid-sentence. The border was the town's whole reason for being and also its great inconvenience, and the townspeople regarded it with the weary affection one gives a difficult but profitable relative who is never, ever going to leave.

subtopic: night arrivals and the dark side of travel
sentence: The bus broke down after dark on an empty road, and we sat in it, the headlights making a small lit world in all the country's blackness, and the romance of overland travel was nowhere to be found. A child cried. The driver swore under the engine. I watched the dark beyond the headlight pool and felt, honestly, afraid, and ashamed of being afraid, and understood that the bright traveller's tales never include enough of these dark patient frightened hours.

subtopic: photographing and trying to capture a place
sentence: The festival was a riot of colour built for the camera and yet the camera kept failing it, freezing the motion that was the whole point, silencing the drums, flattening the crowd's electric warmth into a still and lifeless brightness. I gave up and joined the crowd instead, and let the festival happen to me rather than through a lens, and what I carried away was not an image but a feeling, which is heavier and lasts longer and cannot be shown to anyone.

subtopic: night arrivals and the dark side of travel
sentence: I got lost after dark in a city I did not know, in a district I had been told to avoid, and the streets, charming by day, had become a maze with a different and colder logic, and every footstep behind me was a question. I do not romanticise this. It is the part of travel the brochures omit. I found my way out eventually, into light and people, and the relief was so total it was almost a happiness, but it was happiness built on fear.

I learned ten words of the language and deployed them constantly and probably wrongly, hello and thank you and beautiful and where, and these ten words, scattered through every transaction, transformed my reception entirely, and I understood that the words were not really for communication but for courtesy, a way of saying I see that this is your country and your tongue and I have not simply expected you to accommodate mine.

An old fisherman taught me, over an afternoon I had not planned, how to read the harbour, the signs in the water and the sky that told him what the next day would bring, and his knowledge was vast and entirely undocumented, the accumulated weather-lore of a life spent watching this one stretch of sea. I have forgotten most of it. But I remember the fact of it, that such knowledge exists, held in such people, learnable only by being there.

The flight home crossed in a few hours a distance the journey out had taken weeks to build, and I watched the route unspool backward beneath the wing, the mountains, the coast, the sea, the whole hard-won geography compressed into an afternoon, and felt the particular vertigo of return, the way the going-out is a slow accumulation and the coming-back a sudden collapse. By dinner I would be home. The trip was already, impossibly, becoming a thing that had happened.

The frontier town was full of people waiting, for permits, for relatives, for the right official to come on shift, and waiting had become its main industry, served by cheap hotels and patient cafés and men who knew, for a fee, how to make a wait shorter. I waited there myself, and joined the town's great patient population, and learned that a frontier is not a line but a wide blurred zone of delay, and the town was its capital.

subtopic: night arrivals and the dark side of travel
sentence: I reached the town after dark and could find nothing open, no food, no room, no welcome, only shuttered streets and the wind, and for an hour I walked them with a rising sense of having miscalculated, of having pushed the day too far. Then a light, a door, a woman who took me in. It ended well. But I have not forgotten that hour of dark uncertainty, and I think a traveller should not; it is the shadow that the bright days are bright against.

The dunes were the colour of a lion and moved like slow water, and the wind kept rubbing out our tracks behind us so that we seemed always to be the first people ever to cross. At the top of each ridge there was another, and another, the horizon a series of held promises. When the sun went down the sand turned to embers and then to ash, and the cold came in like a tide, and the stars were so many they frightened me.

The roadside stall sold only tea and only one kind, brewed thick and sweet in a blackened pot, and the man who sold it had a bench and a tarpaulin and a clientele of everyone who passed. I stopped because everyone stopped. The tea was scalding and excellent. Around the bench the conversation was the road's conversation, distances and conditions and the price of fuel, and I sipped and listened and was, for one glass of tea, a local of the road.

The bus station at five in the morning was a small chaos of touts and engines and the smell of the first tea, and finding the right bus was a matter of shouting destinations and trusting the answers. Once aboard, wedged by my pack, I felt the particular settled calm of having committed to a direction. The bus would go where it went. My only job now, for the next nine hours, was to watch the country come.

subtopic: crowds, fairs, and the press of people
sentence: The fairground at night was a crowd lit by a thousand coloured bulbs, the noise enormous, the air thick with frying and diesel and sugar, and the press of people moved between the rides and the stalls in a slow happy churn, and I moved with it. The fair was loud and cheap and a little garish and entirely, infectiously joyful, and the crowd, all of it, every face, had come simply to be happy together, and was, and I, in its midst, was too.

The village faced the lake the way other villages face a square, the water its forum and its livelihood and its weather, and life proceeded along the shore at the unhurried pace of something that has been beside still water for a very long time. I rented a room with a window full of lake, and woke each morning to its flat grey patience, and felt my own restlessness slowly settle, like silt, to the bottom of me.

subtopic: why we go, and the question of travel itself
sentence: I have wondered, on hard nights in cheap rooms, whether the travelling was a way of running from something, and I think, honestly, that it sometimes was, and that this is not the disgrace it is made out to be. We are allowed to need motion. We are allowed to find, in the road, a thing that the settled life withholds. The running, if that is what it was, also showed me the world, and the world, in return, slowly cured me of the need to run.

The lantern festival sent its lights up from the river at dusk, hundreds of them, then thousands, each carrying a wish I could not read written by a hand I would never know. They rose unevenly, the way hope does, some catching and climbing, some failing into the water. I bought one from a girl on the bank and let it go, and watched it join the slow gold migration upward until I genuinely could not tell my light from the rest.

There was nothing to do in the small town and so I did nothing, expertly, for a whole afternoon: sat, watched, drank coffee, watched, walked the river, watched. The town did not mind. It had no expectations to disappoint. And in the doing of nothing, in the long unstructured hours of it, the town slowly revealed itself, the way a quiet person does, and by evening I knew it, and liked it, and was sorry, genuinely sorry, that the morning bus would take me on.

The rock-cut tombs glowed pink at sunset, the whole carved valley taking the low light and holding it, and I walked the floor of it as the shadows climbed the cliffs, among facades a vanished people had cut from the living rock as a way of arguing with death. They had lost the argument, of course; everyone does. But the arguing was magnificent, and it was still here, still beautiful, still saying something to the dusk.

The shepherd I fell into step with on the mountain track taught me, without meaning to, simply by answering my questions, the names of the plants, the use of each one, the way the season was read in the grass, and by the time our paths diverged the mountain had become, for me, a different and far richer place, legible where it had been merely scenic. He waved and went up; I went down, carrying his whole inadvertent lesson.

The train delivered me into a city I knew nothing of, at an hour I had not chosen, and I stood for a moment on the concourse simply absorbing the shock of it: the new alphabet, the new smell, the particular pitch of a crowd speaking a language I did not have. Then I shouldered the pack and walked out into it, into the bright loud unknown, with the specific terror and joy that only a first hour in a strange city gives.
